newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew heads for Hubble service call.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew heads for Hubble service call.

text.p: The space shuttle Discovery streaked a blazing trail across the Florida night sky on Tuesday, heading for a service call to the Hubble Space Telescope.
The $2 billion reusable spaceship and a crew of seven astronauts, blasted off from its seaside launch pad at the Kennedy Space Centre on schedule at 3:55 a.m. EST (0855 GMT).

The thundering launch began a two-day chase through space to catch Hubble for an orbital tune-up that includes the installation of two new scientific instruments and upgrades to various ageing components.
"With a little luck in a couple of weeks the best telescope in the universe will be even better than it is now," said shuttle commander Ken Bowersox, minutes before the shuttle's blastoff.
Also aboard were pilot Scott Horowitz, robot arm operator Steve Hawley and spacewalkers Mark Lee, Steve Smith, Gregory Harbaugh and Joe Tanner.

Discovery's crew was to go to bed 7 1/2 hours after reaching space, with Hubble orbiting about 5,000 miles (8,000 km) ahead of them. During their second day aloft they planned to check their spacesuits and test the shuttle's mechanical arm.

Hawley will use the Canadian-built arm on Thursday to capture the telescope and berth it in the cargo bay for the service work. Hawley, a 45-year-old astrophysicist who returned to the astronaut corps for this mission, released the telescope into space nearly seven years ago.
During four spacewalks, the astronauts will fit the telescope with a multipurpose infrared camera, an improved spectrograph, a sensitive guidance sensor and various upgraded electronics boxes.
The shuttle crew also plan to fire the shuttle's manoeuvring jets to gently ease the telescope into a higher orbit to prolong its lifetime.

"The prime goal of this second servicing mission is a major upgrade, an extension of the science," Hubble chief scientist Ed Weiler said. "We are replacing 1970s technology in our science instruments with 1990s technology."
Astronomers said the new instruments would allow them to see further into the universe, discover new black holes, and peer through veils of dust to see newborn stars.

The astronauts will treat the $2 billion observatory with the greatest of care. Its fragile, electricity-generating solar arrays could buckle if stressed during the refurbishment work. Without power the telescope would be rendered useless.
"There are risks in this mission," Weiler said. "We have to have four successful six-hour spacewalks. It's not just a trip to grandma's to fix her VCR."

The last service crew to visit Hubble was tasked not only with repairing its blurred vision, but restoring NASA's reputation, tarnished by a series of embarrassing failures. Discovery's astronauts faced a different kind of pressure in that they risk damaging a telescope that has made almost daily discoveries and exceeded astronomers' wildest hopes.
"Goal number one is to do no harm," Bowersox said in a prelaunch interview. "Goal number two is to make it better."
If all goes according to plan the new instruments will beam back their first pictures and data about 10 weeks after the shuttle crew returns the telescope to orbit.
